title: Public Policy and British Politics
topics: Parliament and government in the UK

notes.body:
Policy process theories explain how issues reach the agenda, how decisions get made and why policy is usually stable but sometimes changes sharply.

The stages heuristic (Lasswell; refined by others) divides policy into agenda-setting, formulation, decision, implementation and evaluation. It is a useful map, but Sabatier criticised it as descriptive rather than causal, and it misses the way stages overlap.

Rationality and incrementalism:
- Simon: decision-makers have bounded rationality, so they 'satisfice' rather than optimise.
- Lindblom (1959), 'The Science of Muddling Through': policy-makers make small, successive adjustments to existing policy (successive limited comparisons), and agreement on the policy itself replaces agreement on goals. Incrementalism suits pluralist bargaining but struggles to explain sudden change.

Explaining change:
- Kingdon (1984), multiple streams: separate problem, policy and politics streams join when a policy window opens. A policy entrepreneur then attaches a ready-made solution to a problem.
- Baumgartner and Jones (1993), punctuated equilibrium: long stability under policy monopolies is broken by bursts of change when new images and venues (committees, courts, levels of government) bring in new actors.
- Sabatier's advocacy coalition framework (1988): coalitions share deep core and policy core beliefs and compete within a subsystem over 10+ years. Change comes from policy-oriented learning, external shocks or negotiated agreements.
- Hall (1993): first-order change alters settings, second-order changes instruments, third-order changes the paradigm. Britain's shift from Keynesianism to monetarism around 1979 is his third-order case.
- Cohen, March and Olsen (1972), garbage can model: in 'organised anarchies' problems, solutions and participants flow independently and decisions come from their timing.

Power and networks:
- Pluralism (Dahl) versus elite and neo-pluralist views. Bachrach and Baratz (1962) added non-decision-making; Lukes (1974) added a third dimension of shaping preferences.
- Policy networks (Rhodes and Marsh, 1992): from tight policy communities (e.g. post-war agriculture: the ministry and the National Farmers' Union) to loose issue networks (Heclo, 1978).
- Path dependence (Pierson, 2000): increasing returns lock in early choices.
- Policy transfer (Dolowitz and Marsh, 2000): ideas borrowed across jurisdictions, such as US welfare-to-work schemes in the UK New Deal.

Worked illustration: the 2007 smoking ban in England fits Kingdon. The problem stream (evidence on second-hand smoke), the policy stream (Ireland's 2004 ban as a tested model) and the politics stream (a Labour majority and a free vote in 2006) came together, and health campaigners acted as entrepreneurs.

Exam pitfalls: do not treat frameworks as competing laws. Each answers different questions (agenda-setting, stability, learning). Apply concepts precisely, for example a 'window' is not just any moment of change. Evaluate the frameworks: they are good at explaining change after it happens but weak at predicting it.

Weber's ideal-type bureaucracy has hierarchy, written rules, specialisation, merit appointment and impersonal administration. Its strength is predictability; its risks include rigidity and goal displacement (Merton).

Public choice and bureaucratic behaviour:
- Niskanen (1971): officials maximise their budgets because pay, prestige and power grow with them, which leads to oversupply.
- Dunleavy (1991), bureau-shaping: senior officials prefer small, elite, policy-focused agencies and hive off delivery work.
- Principal–agent theory: ministers (principals) struggle to monitor officials (agents) who have better information.

The UK civil service: the Northcote–Trevelyan Report (1854) set up permanent, politically neutral, merit-based officials. Ministerial responsibility, together with the Carltona principle (Carltona v Commissioners of Works, 1943), means officials act in the minister's name. The Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010 put the civil service on a statutory footing. Tension over special advisers and the dismissal of permanent secretaries raises questions about politicisation.

New Public Management (Hood, 1991): private-sector methods such as targets, agencies, contracting-out and performance pay. The Next Steps report (Ibbs, 1988) moved delivery into executive agencies. Rhodes (1994) warned of a 'hollowing out' of the state, and later 'governance' accounts stress steering networks rather than rowing. Dunleavy et al. (2006) describe a turn to digital-era governance.

Implementation:
- Pressman and Wildavsky (1973) studied a federal job-creation programme in Oakland. Many decision points and the need for clearances meant small chances of failure at each step added up to near-certain delay.
- Top-down (Sabatier and Mazmanian): clear objectives, a sound causal theory, enough resources and committed officials. Hood (1976) set out the conditions for 'perfect administration'.
- Bottom-up: Lipsky (1980) showed that street-level bureaucrats such as teachers, police officers and benefits staff in effect make policy through discretion as they ration scarce time. Elmore's (1979) 'backward mapping' starts from the point of delivery.

Worked example: suppose a programme needs 10 independent clearances, each with a 95% chance of success. The overall probability is 0.95¹⁰ ≈ 0.60. With 20 clearances it falls to about 0.36. This is Pressman and Wildavsky's arithmetic of joint action.

British illustration: the poll tax (Community Charge), introduced in Scotland in 1989 and in England and Wales in 1990, failed through poor design, collection problems and mass non-payment, and was replaced by council tax in 1993 (Butler, Adonis and Travers, 1994). King and Crewe (2013) blamed blunders on 'cultural disconnect', weak scrutiny and ministers who move on quickly.

Exam pitfalls: implementation failure is not always the bureaucracy's fault, because flawed policy design often lies upstream. Avoid treating top-down and bottom-up as simply right or wrong, since synthesis models (Matland's 1995 ambiguity–conflict matrix) say which fits which kind of policy.

notes.h: Parliament and government in the UK
notes.body:
The UK has a parliamentary system and an uncodified constitution resting on parliamentary sovereignty (Dicey). The government is drawn from and accountable to Parliament, but a single-party majority usually controls the Commons. Lord Hailsham called this an 'elective dictatorship' (1976).

The core executive (Dunleavy and Rhodes, 1990) is the network of the Prime Minister, Cabinet, committees, the Treasury, the Cabinet Office and senior officials that coordinates policy. Debates on prime ministerial power:
- Prime ministerial government (Crossman, 1963) and the 'British presidency' thesis (Foley, 1993; 2000).
- Cabinet constraints: the PM depends on colleagues and the party. Thatcher (1990), May (2019), Johnson (2022) and Truss (2022) were all forced out by their own parties, not by voters.
- Heffernan: power is contingent on resources such as electoral success, party standing and the media.

Parliament's functions are legitimation, scrutiny, representation, recruiting ministers and law-making.
- Legislation: public bills pass through second reading, committee (public bill committees), report and third reading in each House, then receive Royal Assent. The Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949 limit the Lords to delay. The Salisbury convention means the Lords does not block manifesto bills at second reading.
- Scrutiny: Prime Minister's Questions, written questions, urgent questions and departmental select committees (since 1979). The Wright reforms (2010) introduced elected chairs and members and a Backbench Business Committee.
- Russell and Cowley (2016) argue that Westminster's policy influence is often underestimated: anticipated reactions, backbench pressure and Lords amendments shape bills before votes take place.

Key statutes and cases: the Dissolution and Calling of Parliament Act 2022 repealed the Fixed-term Parliaments Act 2011 and restored the prerogative power of dissolution. In R (Miller) v Secretary of State for Exiting the EU [2017] UKSC 5 the Supreme Court held that Parliament had to authorise the Article 50 notification. In R (Miller) v Prime Minister; Cherry v Advocate General [2019] UKSC 41 it held that the 2019 prorogation was unlawful.

The Lords: the House of Lords Act 1999 removed most hereditary peers, leaving 92, and the House of Lords (Hereditary Peers) Act 2026 (Royal Assent March 2026, in force from 29 April 2026) removed the rest, although some were then returned as life peers. The Lords revises bills, and its expertise and lack of an elected mandate shape its restraint.

Illustration: in June 2025 more than 100 Labour MPs signed a reasoned amendment opposing planned welfare cuts. The government conceded and, on 1 July 2025, dropped its proposed restrictions on Personal Independence Payment eligibility pending a review, despite a majority of over 160. Backbench power works mostly through the threat of rebellion rather than actual defeats.

Exam pitfalls: do not equate a large majority with unlimited power. Separate formal powers from conventions. Use recent examples rather than relying on Bagehot's 'efficient secret' alone.

Electoral systems in the UK:
- Westminster: first past the post in 650 constituencies.
- Scottish Parliament: additional member system, with 73 constituency and 56 regional list MSPs. List seats are allocated by a modified D'Hondt formula that counts constituency seats already won.
- Senedd: since the May 2026 election, 96 members elected by closed-list PR (D'Hondt) in 16 six-member constituencies (Senedd Cymru (Members and Elections) Act 2024).
- Northern Ireland Assembly and local elections in Scotland and Northern Ireland: single transferable vote.
- The 2011 alternative vote referendum was rejected 67.9% to 32.1%. The Elections Act 2022 introduced photo ID at polling stations and switched mayoral and PCC elections to FPTP. The English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act 2026 restored the supplementary vote for mayoral elections after the May 2026 contests.

Explaining vote choice:
- Class alignment: Pulzer (1967) saw class as the basis of British party politics; Butler and Stokes (1969) linked it to inherited party identification.
- Dealignment: Särlvik and Crewe (1983) documented class and partisan dealignment from the 1970s. Heath, Jowell and Curtice (1985) countered that relative class voting had fallen less than absolute measures suggested.
- Issue and valence voting: Clarke, Sanders, Stewart and Whiteley (2004) argued that judgements of competence, leader images and partisanship as a running tally best explain choice. The 1992 ERM crisis wrecked the Conservatives' reputation for economic competence.
- Electoral Shocks (Fieldhouse et al., 2019): shocks such as the financial crisis, immigration, the Scottish independence referendum and Brexit have increased volatility.
- New divides: age and education now predict vote choice better than class. In 2017 and 2019 age was the strongest predictor. Sobolewska and Ford (2020) describe identity conflict between graduate 'identity liberals' and older, non-graduate 'identity conservatives'.

The 2024 general election: Labour won 411 seats on 33.7% of the vote, the Conservatives 121 on 23.7%, the Liberal Democrats 72 on 12.2%, Reform UK 5 on 14.3%, and the Greens 4. Turnout was about 60%. It was the most disproportional result on record: no single-party majority had rested on so low a vote share.

Worked example (AMS): in a seven-seat Scottish region, Party A wins 7 constituencies and Party B wins 2. List votes are A 118,000, B 91,000, C 62,000 and D 29,000. The divisor is list votes ÷ (seats already won + 1). A's first quotient is 118,000 ÷ 8 = 14,750, while C's is 62,000. After seven rounds C wins 3 list seats, B 3, D 1 and A none. This compensation corrects A's constituency over-representation.

Exam pitfalls: do not claim class no longer matters, since it has realigned with manual workers moving right. Separate turnout from vote choice. Remember that 'dealignment' covers both partisan and class dealignment. Treat 2024 as a fragmented, low-enthusiasm result rather than a realignment like 1997.

Origins and ideas:
- The Conservatives combine one-nation paternalism (Disraeli, Macmillan), Thatcherite neo-liberalism and, more recently, national populism on immigration and sovereignty. Bale traces how the party has dealt with Europe, modernisation and the radical right.
- Labour grew out of the Labour Representation Committee (1900), linking trade unions and socialist societies. Blair's 1995 rewrite of Clause IV dropped the commitment to common ownership, and New Labour adopted a 'third way' (Giddens).
- The Liberal Democrats (formed 1988 from the Liberals and SDP) joined the 2010–15 coalition, then fell from 57 seats to 8.
- Nationalist parties: the SNP (governing in Scotland since 2007) and Plaid Cymru. In Northern Ireland the party system runs along unionist and nationalist lines (DUP, Sinn Féin, UUP, SDLP, Alliance).
- Challengers: UKIP pushed for the 2016 referendum. The Brexit Party (2019) renamed itself Reform UK in 2021. Under Farage it won 14.3% and five seats in 2024 and, in May 2025, won control of several county councils and the Runcorn and Helsby by-election.

Internal power:
- McKenzie (1955) argued that power in both main parties lay with the parliamentary leadership regardless of formal rules.
- Leadership selection: Conservative MPs reduce the field to two, then members choose. Members picked Truss over Sunak in 2022 and Badenoch over Jenrick in 2024. Labour moved to one member one vote with registered supporters (Collins Review, 2014), which helped Corbyn win in 2015. Nomination thresholds were later raised to 20% of MPs.
- Members are older, more middle-class and more ideological than voters (Bale, Webb and Poletti, 2020).

Party system change: Britain's two-party dominance in votes peaked in 1951, when Labour and the Conservatives took about 97% of the vote, and has since fragmented. FPTP still props up the two-party share of seats. The effective number of electoral parties has risen sharply since 2015, and multi-party competition at constituency level now creates unpredictable results.

Finance and regulation: the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000 set up the Electoral Commission, banned foreign donations, required donations to be reported and capped campaign spending. Opposition parties receive Short money (from 1975). State funding remains limited compared with continental Europe.

Worked example: in 2024 Labour and the Conservatives together won about 57% of the vote, a post-war low, yet 82% of seats (532 of 650). The gap shows how FPTP shields a fragmenting party system.

Exam pitfalls: separate ideology from organisation. Do not claim the Conservatives are purely Thatcherite, since internal factions persist. Note that party membership numbers fluctuate. Use the cartel and catch-all frameworks critically when analysing British parties.

Devolution transferred power without giving up parliamentary sovereignty. It is asymmetric, and England has no parliament of its own.

Scotland: after the 1997 referendum, the Scotland Act 1998 set up a Parliament with all powers not reserved to Westminster. The Scotland Acts 2012 and 2016 (following the Smith Commission) added income tax powers and some welfare powers. The 2014 independence referendum produced 55.3% for No. In Reference re Scottish Independence Referendum Bill [2022] UKSC 31 the Supreme Court held that Holyrood cannot legislate for a referendum without Westminster's consent. In 2023 the UK government used a section 35 order for the first time to block the Gender Recognition Reform (Scotland) Bill, and the Court of Session upheld it.

Wales: the 1997 referendum was won narrowly (50.3%). The Government of Wales Act 1998 created an executive-style Assembly, primary law-making followed the 2011 referendum, and the Wales Act 2017 introduced a reserved-powers model. The Senedd and Elections (Wales) Act 2020 renamed it the Senedd and lowered the voting age to 16, and the 2024 Act expanded it to 96 members.

Northern Ireland: the Belfast/Good Friday Agreement (1998) and the Northern Ireland Act 1998 set up consociational power-sharing (Lijphart). Features include a cross-community First and deputy First Minister, ministries allocated by D'Hondt, and petitions of concern. The institutions collapsed in 2017–20 and 2022–24, returning in February 2024 with Sinn Féin's Michelle O'Neill as First Minister.

Constitutional glue:
- Sewel convention: Westminster will not normally legislate on devolved matters without consent. The Scotland Act 2016 put it in statute, but in Miller (2017) the Supreme Court held that it is not legally enforceable.
- The Barnett formula (1978) adjusts devolved block grants in line with comparable spending changes in England, by population share. It is criticised for not reflecting need.
- The UK Internal Market Act 2020 strengthened the centre, which devolved governments call a power grab.

England: regional assemblies were dropped after the North East's 2004 referendum rejected one (78% No). Combined authorities with metro mayors have grown since 2014 through deal-based devolution. The English Devolution White Paper (2024) and the English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act 2026 aim to give every area a strategic authority.

Theory: Hooghe and Marks (2001) separate Type I (general-purpose, nested) from Type II (task-specific, overlapping) multi-level governance. Bulpitt's 'territorial code' described the centre managing 'high politics' while leaving 'low politics' to local elites. Ron Davies called devolution 'a process, not an event', and scholars debate whether the UK is now quasi-federal.

Exam pitfalls: devolved powers are not entrenched. Abolishing Holyrood is legally possible but politically unthinkable. Do not describe Northern Ireland's model as simply devolution, because it is consociational and international.

Road to the referendum: Cameron promised the referendum in his Bloomberg speech (2013) to manage Conservative divisions and the rise of UKIP. The vote was held on 23 June 2016. Leave won 51.9% to 48.1% on a turnout of 72.2%. England and Wales voted Leave; Scotland (62% Remain) and Northern Ireland (55.8% Remain) voted Remain.

Explaining the vote:
- 'Left behind' thesis: Ford and Goodwin (2014) and Goodwin and Heath (2016) found that older, white, non-graduate voters in post-industrial areas voted Leave.
- Values and identity: education, attitudes to immigration, authoritarian–libertarian values and English identity predicted the vote better than income (Hobolt, 2016; Sobolewska and Ford, 2020).
- Campaign: Clarke, Goodwin and Whiteley (2017) stress leaders, risk perceptions and 'take back control'.

Process and Parliament:
- May triggered Article 50 on 29 March 2017, after Miller [2017] UKSC 5 required an Act. The European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018 repealed the European Communities Act 1972 and converted EU law into domestic 'retained' law.
- The 2017 election lost May her majority, leaving her reliant on the DUP's confidence and supply. Her Withdrawal Agreement was defeated by 230 votes on 15 January 2019, the largest government defeat in modern history. The Northern Ireland backstop was central to the deadlock.
- Parliament took control of the order paper, and the European Union (Withdrawal) (No. 2) Act 2019 (the 'Benn Act') required an extension request to avoid no deal. The Supreme Court ruled the prorogation unlawful in Miller/Cherry [2019] UKSC 41.
- Johnson renegotiated, replacing the backstop with the Northern Ireland Protocol, which placed a customs and regulatory border in the Irish Sea. The December 2019 election produced an 80-seat majority. The UK left on 31 January 2020, the transition ended on 31 December 2020, and the Trade and Cooperation Agreement provided zero-tariff, zero-quota goods trade but little for services.

Aftermath:
- The Windsor Framework (2023) created green and red lanes and the 'Stormont brake'. The Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023 renamed retained law 'assimilated law' from 2024.
- The Labour government's 'reset': the May 2025 UK–EU summit agreed a security and defence partnership and opened talks on a veterinary (SPS) agreement and youth mobility. Rejoining the single market or customs union is ruled out.

Worked illustration: Brexit pitted popular sovereignty against parliamentary sovereignty. In the March–April 2019 indicative votes no option won a majority: a Parliament able to block outcomes but not agree one.

Exam pitfalls: do not reduce the vote to economics or immigration alone. Distinguish the Withdrawal Agreement (exit terms) from the TCA (the future relationship). Remember that Leave and Remain identities (Hobolt, Leeper and Tilley, 2021) outlasted 2016 and reshaped party competition in 2019.

Origins: the Beveridge Report (1942) targeted five 'giants': Want, Disease, Ignorance, Squalor and Idleness. The post-war settlement included the National Insurance Act 1946 (contributory benefits), the NHS (founded 1948, free at the point of use), the Education Act 1944 and a commitment to full employment. Marshall (1950) saw social rights as the third stage of citizenship after civil and political rights.

Comparative frameworks:
- Esping-Andersen (1990) identified three worlds of welfare capitalism, compared by decommodification (independence from the market) and stratification. Liberal regimes (US, UK) rely on means-tested benefits and markets. Conservative-corporatist regimes (Germany, France) use status-preserving social insurance. Social democratic regimes (Sweden, Denmark) offer universal, generous benefits. The UK is a hybrid: a universal NHS alongside residual cash benefits.
- Feminist critiques (Lewis, 1992; Orloff) note the male-breadwinner assumptions and the neglect of care work.
- Titmuss contrasted universalism with selectivity: means-testing stigmatises and risks the poverty trap, while universal services build cross-class support.

The politics of retrenchment:
- Pierson (1994): cutting welfare is not the mirror image of building it. Beneficiaries form concentrated constituencies, so governments pursue blame avoidance and hidden cuts. Thatcher's record supports this, since spending on core programmes proved hard to cut, although uprating pensions by prices from 1980 and the sale of council housing were significant.
- New social risks (Taylor-Gooby, 2004): lone parenthood, care needs and insecure work strain systems built for male industrial risks. Social investment approaches (Hemerijck) focus on childcare and skills.

UK policy since 1997: New Labour's tax credits, the minimum wage (1998) and welfare-to-work. The coalition's austerity included the benefit cap (2013) and Universal Credit (Welfare Reform Act 2012), which merges six means-tested benefits into one payment with a taper. The two-child limit (2017) restricted child-related support; after fierce argument within Labour, the November 2025 Budget lifted it from April 2026. The pensions triple lock (from 2011) raises the state pension by the highest of earnings growth, CPI inflation or 2.5%.

Worked example (triple lock): if CPI is 1.7%, earnings growth 4.8%, and the floor 2.5%, the pension rises by 4.8%. On a weekly pension of £200, that adds £9.60, giving £209.60. Because the lock ratchets the pension up relative to earnings, its cost keeps growing, yet governments fear dropping it.

Universal Credit's taper has been 55% since 2021: each extra £100 of net earnings (after income tax and NI) above the work allowance cuts UC by £55, leaving £45.

Exam pitfalls: separate spending levels from regime type, since generosity, conditionality and universality matter. Do not assume retrenchment is easy or that 'austerity' cut everything equally; pensioners were protected while working-age benefits fell. Link policy to electoral politics: older voters have high turnout.

cards.f: What are the stages of the policy cycle heuristic?
cards.b: Agenda-setting, formulation, decision-making, implementation and evaluation, sometimes followed by termination or succession.
Policy-makers 'muddle through' by making small, successive changes to existing policy, comparing limited options rather than reviewing all possibilities.

Problems (conditions defined as needing action), policies (solutions developed by specialists) and politics (national mood, elections, interest groups). Change happens when they meet in a policy window.
In Kingdon's model, an actor who invests time and resources to attach a favoured solution to a problem when a policy window opens.
Long periods of stability under policy monopolies are interrupted by rapid change when new policy images and venues mobilise previously excluded actors.

cards.f: Advocacy coalition framework: main sources of policy change
cards.b: Policy-oriented learning, external shocks (e.g. economic crises, changes of government), internal shocks and negotiated agreements between coalitions.

cards.f: Hall's three orders of policy change
cards.b: First order: instrument settings change. Second order: instruments themselves change. Third order: the overarching goals or paradigm change.
A policy community is a small, stable, closed network with shared values (e.g. post-war agriculture). An issue network is large, fluid and conflictual (Rhodes and Marsh; Heclo).
Decision-making (open conflict), non-decision-making (keeping issues off the agenda) and shaping preferences so that grievances never arise.
Early choices generate increasing returns, such as adaptation, vested interests and learning, which make it costly to reverse course later.
A hierarchy of offices, rule-governed conduct, specialisation, written records, appointment and promotion by merit, and impersonal administration.
Bureaucrats seek to maximise their agency budgets because personal rewards rise with them, leading to oversupply of public services.
Senior officials prefer small, collegial, policy-focused agencies over large budgets, so they hive off delivery functions to agencies or contractors.
Applying private-sector techniques to government: performance targets, executive agencies, competition, contracting-out and managerial discretion.
The Ibbs report that led to executive agencies separating delivery from policy, with chief executives accountable for performance against targets.

cards.f: What did Pressman and Wildavsky (1973) show?
cards.b: In Oakland, a federal programme needed many clearances from many actors, and even high success odds at each point multiplied into probable failure or delay.
Front-line workers such as teachers, police and caseworkers exercise discretion under resource pressure, so in practice they make policy in delivering it.
Top-down asks how far outcomes match central objectives. Bottom-up starts from front-line actors and local networks to see how policy is actually shaped.

Four implementation types: administrative (low ambiguity, low conflict), political (low ambiguity, high conflict), experimental (high ambiguity, low conflict) and symbolic (high ambiguity, high conflict).

cards.f: King and Crewe's causes of policy blunders (2013)
cards.b: Including cultural disconnect between ministers and those affected, group-think, weak parliamentary scrutiny, ministerial churn and a deficit of deliberation.
Officials can exercise powers given to ministers, with the minister remaining accountable to Parliament (Carltona v Commissioners of Works, 1943).

cards.f: What is the 'core executive' (Dunleavy and Rhodes, 1990)?
cards.b: The complex of organisations and procedures, including the PM, Cabinet, committees, the Treasury, the Cabinet Office and senior officials, that coordinates and arbitrates central government policy.
A government with a Commons majority, under an uncodified constitution with weak checks, can pass almost anything it wishes between elections.

cards.f: What did the Wright reforms (2010) change?
cards.b: Select committee chairs elected by the whole House and members elected by party groups, plus a Backbench Business Committee controlling some Commons time.
They limit the Lords to delaying most public bills by about one year and money bills by one month, after which the Commons can pass them without Lords consent.
The Lords does not block at second reading government bills that carry out a manifesto commitment.

cards.f: Dissolution and Calling of Parliament Act 2022
cards.b: Repealed the Fixed-term Parliaments Act 2011, revived the prerogative power to dissolve Parliament and made its exercise non-justiciable.
Prorogation is unlawful if it frustrates Parliament's constitutional functions without reasonable justification, and the 2019 five-week prorogation was null.

cards.f: Russell and Cowley's (2016) argument about Westminster
cards.b: Parliament's policy influence is underestimated, since it works largely through anticipated reactions, backbench pressure and changes before votes.
Prime ministers increasingly lead in a presidential style, through 'spatial leadership' that distances them from party and government, and media personalisation.

cards.f: Which PMs since 1990 were forced out by their own party rather than voters?
cards.b: Thatcher (1990), May (2019), Johnson (2022) and Truss (2022).
Rejected, 67.9% to 32.1%, so FPTP was kept for Westminster elections.
Partisan dealignment is the weakening of party identification. Class dealignment is the weakening link between social class and vote choice. Both rose from the 1970s (Särlvik and Crewe, 1983).

cards.f: Valence model of British voting (Clarke et al., 2004)
cards.b: Voters choose on judgements of which party is most competent on shared goals such as growth and public services, shaped by leader images and partisan cues.

cards.f: Strongest demographic predictors of vote in 2017–19
cards.b: Age and education, which overtook class. Younger graduates leaned Labour; older non-graduates leaned Conservative.

cards.f: 2024 general election seats and vote shares
cards.b: Labour 411 seats (33.7%), Conservatives 121 (23.7%), Liberal Democrats 72 (12.2%), Reform UK 5 (14.3%), Greens 4.

cards.f: How are Scottish Parliament list seats allocated?
cards.b: Modified D'Hondt: each party's regional list vote is divided by (constituency seats won in the region + list seats already allocated + 1).

cards.f: What did the Elections Act 2022 change?
cards.b: It introduced photo voter ID in Great Britain and switched mayoral and Police and Crime Commissioner elections to FPTP. The English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act 2026 later restored the supplementary vote for mayors.
96 members in 16 six-member constituencies, elected by closed-list PR using D'Hondt.

cards.f: Heath, Jowell and Curtice's (1985) challenge to dealignment
cards.b: Absolute class voting fell partly because the class structure changed. Relative class voting, measured by odds ratios, declined much less.
Major events such as the financial crisis, immigration, Scottish independence and Brexit disrupted party loyalties and raised volatility.
Blair replaced Labour's commitment to common ownership of the means of production with a statement of democratic socialist values.
Despite different constitutions, power in both the Conservative and Labour parties lay with the parliamentary leadership.

cards.f: How does the Conservative Party choose its leader?
cards.b: MPs vote in successive rounds to narrow the field to two, then party members choose between them, as with Truss in 2022 and Badenoch in 2024.
Labour moved to one member one vote, including registered supporters, which helped Corbyn win in 2015.

cards.f: Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000
cards.b: Created the Electoral Commission, banned foreign donations, required reporting of large donations and capped national campaign spending.
State funding for opposition parties in the Commons, introduced in 1975, to support their parliamentary work.
The Brexit Party, founded in 2019, renamed itself Reform UK in 2021. Under Farage it won 14.3% and five seats in 2024.

cards.f: Why does FPTP sustain two-party dominance in seats despite fragmenting votes?
cards.b: Votes for third parties spread thinly across seats win few constituencies, so the two largest parties win a far higher share of seats than votes.
Their seats fell from 57 to 8 in 2015, punished for the tuition-fee U-turn and coalition with the Conservatives. They recovered to 72 seats in 2024 through targeted campaigning.

cards.f: How do party members differ from voters (Bale, Webb and Poletti, 2020)?
cards.b: Members are older, more middle-class and more ideological, which matters because they choose leaders.
A reserved-powers model: the Scottish Parliament can legislate on anything not reserved to Westminster in Schedule 5.
Westminster will not normally legislate on devolved matters without the consent of the devolved legislature. It is stated in statute but not legally enforceable (Miller, 2017).

cards.f: What did the Supreme Court decide in the 2022 Scottish referendum reference?
cards.b: An independence referendum relates to reserved matters (the Union and the UK Parliament), so Holyrood cannot legislate for one without Westminster's agreement.
Adjusts devolved block grants in proportion to population when comparable spending in England changes. Criticised for ignoring relative need.

cards.f: Consociational features of the Good Friday Agreement
cards.b: Joint First and deputy First Ministers, executive posts allocated by D'Hondt, cross-community voting and petitions of concern, and proportional representation by STV.
The UK government's first use of the Scotland Act power to block a bill from Royal Assent, applied to the Gender Recognition Reform (Scotland) Bill.
Voters rejected an elected regional assembly by about 78% to 22%, ending Labour's plan for English regional government.

cards.f: Type I v Type II multi-level governance
cards.b: Type I: general-purpose, territorially nested jurisdictions (local, devolved, national). Type II: task-specific, overlapping bodies (Hooghe and Marks).
Requires goods and services lawfully sold in one UK nation to be accepted in the others. Devolved governments say it limits their policy choices.
The centre controlled 'high politics' (defence, the economy) and left 'low politics' to local elites, managing the periphery at arm's length.
Leave 51.9%, Remain 48.1%, turnout 72.2%. Scotland and Northern Ireland voted Remain.
The government could not trigger Article 50 using prerogative powers alone, because withdrawal would change domestic law and rights. An Act of Parliament was needed.
May's insurance plan to avoid a hard Irish border: the UK would stay in a customs union with the EU until alternative arrangements were found.
Johnson's 2019 replacement for the backstop: Northern Ireland follows EU goods rules and customs code, with checks on goods from Great Britain at its ports.
Revised the Protocol with green and red lanes for goods and a 'Stormont brake' letting the Assembly object to new EU goods rules.

cards.f: Withdrawal Agreement v Trade and Cooperation Agreement
cards.b: The Withdrawal Agreement (2019–20) set the exit terms: money, citizens' rights and Northern Ireland. The TCA (December 2020) governs the future relationship, including zero-tariff goods trade.
