questions.q: Using Kingdon's multiple streams framework, explain how the ban on smoking in enclosed public places in England (2007) came about.
markScheme: Problem stream: growing evidence of harm from second-hand smoke and public concern
Policy stream: a viable, tested solution (e.g. Ireland's 2004 and Scotland's 2006 bans)
Politics stream: a Labour government with a large majority and changing public mood; a free vote in 2006 extended the ban
Coupling through a policy window, with health campaigners (e.g. ASH, BMA) acting as entrepreneurs
questions.modelAnswer: In the problem stream, evidence on the health effects of second-hand smoke, especially for hospitality workers, defined passive smoking as a problem rather than a matter of personal choice. In the policy stream, Ireland's 2004 ban and Scotland's 2006 ban gave a tested solution and showed that predicted economic damage had not happened. In the politics stream, a Labour government with a large majority and a public increasingly opposed to smoking made action feasible. When the government's initial plan exempted some pubs, MPs voted on a free vote in 2006 for a comprehensive ban. Health groups such as ASH and the BMA acted as policy entrepreneurs, linking the streams when the window opened.

questions.q: Compare the advocacy coalition framework with punctuated equilibrium theory as explanations of policy change.
markScheme: ACF: coalitions defined by shared belief systems compete within a subsystem; change through learning or external shocks over 10+ years
PET: long stability under policy monopolies, then sudden bursts when images and venues change
Contrast: ACF emphasises beliefs and gradual learning; PET emphasises attention, agenda dynamics and institutional venues
Evaluative point: e.g. both struggle to predict when change happens; ACF was built on US subsystems; PET's distribution of policy changes is empirically well supported
questions.modelAnswer: Sabatier's ACF explains policy through coalitions of actors who share deep core and policy core beliefs and compete within a subsystem over a decade or more. Core beliefs resist change, so major shifts usually need external shocks, while learning adjusts secondary beliefs. Baumgartner and Jones's punctuated equilibrium explains long stability under policy monopolies broken by sudden change when new policy images attract attention and issues move to new venues. The ACF focuses on beliefs and gradual learning, while PET focuses on attention and institutions. Both explain change well after the fact but find it hard to predict when it will occur.

questions.q: Explain the main criticisms of New Public Management in the UK.
markScheme: Fragmentation and loss of coordination ('hollowing out', Rhodes 1994)
Accountability gaps between ministers and agency chief executives (e.g. the 1995 Howard–Lewis Prison Service dispute)
Gaming and perverse incentives from targets (e.g. NHS waiting-time targets)
Contracting-out risks and market failure (e.g. Carillion's collapse in 2018)
Erosion of public service ethos and equity concerns; shift to post-NPM or 'joined-up' governance
questions.modelAnswer: NPM broke the state into agencies and contracts, which Rhodes (1994) called a 'hollowing out' that weakened central coordination. Separating policy from operations blurred accountability: in 1995 Home Secretary Michael Howard sacked Prison Service head Derek Lewis after prison escapes, and the two disputed where responsibility lay. Targets encouraged gaming, as with hospitals managing NHS waiting-time measures rather than patient need. Outsourcing exposed the state to market failure, shown by Carillion's collapse in 2018. Critics also argue that NPM eroded the public service ethos and focused on efficiency over equity, prompting New Labour's 'joined-up government'.

questions.q: Explain two ways in which the House of Commons scrutinises the executive.
markScheme: Identifies one method with explanation (e.g. departmental select committees questioning ministers and officials and publishing reports)
Identifies a second method with explanation (e.g. PMQs, written and urgent questions, opposition days, Liaison Committee)
Provides an assessment or example of effectiveness
questions.modelAnswer: Departmental select committees, set up in 1979, examine each department's spending, administration and policy. They take evidence from ministers and officials and publish reports to which the government must respond. Since the Wright reforms (2010) their chairs have been elected by the whole House, giving them more independence and authority. Questions to ministers, including Prime Minister's Questions and urgent questions granted by the Speaker, force ministers to explain themselves in public. PMQs is often more theatre than scrutiny, but committee work, such as inquiries into the Windrush scandal, has exposed serious failings.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by partisan dealignment and give two pieces of evidence for it in Britain.
markScheme: Defines partisan dealignment: weakening of voters' psychological attachment to parties
Evidence 1: fall in strength of party identification in BES data since the 1960s
Evidence 2: rising volatility and vote switching between elections (Fieldhouse et al.)
Evidence 3: declining combined two-party share (e.g. about 57% in 2024 against about 97% in 1951) or the success of new parties
questions.modelAnswer: Partisan dealignment means voters' long-term psychological attachment to a party is weakening, so loyalty no longer anchors their vote. British Election Study data show that the share of voters who identify 'very strongly' with a party has fallen sharply since the 1960s. Individual-level switching between elections reached record levels in the 2010s (Fieldhouse et al., 2019). The combined Labour and Conservative vote share has dropped from about 97% in 1951 to about 57% in 2024, while challengers such as UKIP, Reform UK and the Greens have won large vote shares.

questions.q: Using the 2024 general election, explain why the UK's party system can be described as 'two-party in seats but multi-party in votes'.
markScheme: Labour and Conservatives won about 57% of the vote combined
They won 532 of 650 seats (about 82%)
Reform UK (about 14% of the vote, 5 seats) and Greens (under 7%, 4 seats) show minor-party penalties under FPTP
Explains the mechanism: the geographic distribution of votes; contrasts with the Lib Dems' efficient 12% for 72 seats
questions.modelAnswer: In 2024 Labour and the Conservatives together won only about 57% of the vote, the lowest combined share since 1945, yet took 532 of 650 seats, around 82%. Reform UK won over 14% of votes but only five seats, and the Greens four, because their support was spread evenly and rarely came first in a constituency. The Liberal Democrats' 12% won 72 seats because their votes were concentrated in target seats. FPTP rewards concentrated support, so a fragmented electorate can still produce a seat distribution dominated by two parties.

questions.q: Explain why devolution in the UK is described as 'asymmetric' and identify one problem this causes.
markScheme: Scotland has a reserved-powers Parliament with tax and some welfare powers
Wales has had legislative powers since 2011 and a reserved-powers model since 2017, but fewer powers (e.g. no justice system)
Northern Ireland has a consociational power-sharing model under an international agreement
England has no devolved legislature; only patchy combined authorities and metro mayors
Problem: the West Lothian/English question; or uneven funding via Barnett; or a lack of a coherent intergovernmental framework
questions.modelAnswer: Devolution is asymmetric because each nation received different arrangements. The Scottish Parliament has broad legislative powers, including income tax rates and some welfare benefits. The Senedd gained primary powers in 2011 and a reserved-powers model in 2017, but criminal justice remains with Westminster. Northern Ireland's Assembly runs a consociational power-sharing system rooted in the Good Friday Agreement. England, with about 84% of the UK population, has no legislature, only combined authorities and metro mayors with deal-based powers. This creates the West Lothian question: Scottish MPs can vote on English-only matters, but English MPs cannot vote on devolved Scottish matters.

questions.q: Explain why Theresa May struggled to get a Brexit deal through Parliament between 2017 and 2019.
markScheme: Loss of majority in 2017 and reliance on the DUP, which opposed the backstop
Conservative divisions: the ERG opposed the backstop as trapping the UK; Remainers sought a softer Brexit or a second referendum
Labour opposition and cross-party demands; no majority for any alternative in the indicative votes
Institutional context: Parliament asserting control (e.g. Grieve amendment, Benn Act), plus the record 230-vote defeat
questions.modelAnswer: May's position collapsed after the 2017 election cost her majority and made her rely on the DUP, which rejected the Northern Ireland backstop as treating the province differently. Conservative Eurosceptics in the European Research Group feared the backstop would keep the UK in a customs union indefinitely, while pro-European Conservatives wanted a softer deal or a referendum. Labour, seeking an election, opposed the deal. The result was a 230-vote defeat in January 2019. Indicative votes then showed no majority for any alternative, which left Parliament able to block but not to decide.

questions.q: Using Esping-Andersen's typology, explain why the UK is often described as a 'hybrid' welfare state.
markScheme: Defines the liberal regime: means-testing, modest flat-rate benefits, market reliance
UK liberal features: means-tested Universal Credit, low replacement rates, conditionality
UK universal or social democratic features: the NHS, free at the point of use and funded by taxation
Concludes on the hybrid nature (Beveridgean universalism in services, residualism in cash benefits)
questions.modelAnswer: Esping-Andersen classified the UK as a liberal regime, marked by means-tested, modest benefits and reliance on the market. Its cash benefits fit: Universal Credit is means-tested and conditional, and the basic state pension and unemployment support replace a low share of earnings compared with continental systems. However, the NHS is a universal, tax-funded service free at the point of use, which is closer to the social democratic model and limits commodification of healthcare. The UK therefore combines Beveridgean universalism in services with a residual, increasingly targeted system of cash benefits.

questions.q: A pensioner receives £200 a week. Over three years, CPI inflation is 3.1%, 10.1% and 1.7%, and earnings growth is 6.0%, 8.5% and 4.1%. Calculate the weekly pension after three years under the triple lock, and compare it with uprating by earnings alone. What does this show?
markScheme: Year 1: uprate by 6.0% (earnings) to £212.00
Year 2: uprate by 10.1% (CPI) to £233.41
Year 3: uprate by 4.1% (earnings) to £242.98
Earnings-only uprating gives £239.45, so the triple lock is £3.53 higher
Explains the ratchet: by taking the highest measure each year, the pension rises faster than earnings over time, increasing fiscal cost
questions.modelAnswer: Under the triple lock, year 1 uses earnings (6.0%): £200 × 1.060 = £212.00. Year 2 uses CPI (10.1%): £212.00 × 1.101 = £233.41. Year 3 uses earnings (4.1%): £233.41 × 1.041 = £242.98. Uprating by earnings alone gives £200 × 1.060 × 1.085 × 1.041 = £239.45. The triple lock pension is about £3.53 a week higher. Because it takes the highest measure each year, it works as a ratchet, so the state pension rises faster than average earnings over time. That explains its growing cost and its electoral importance to older voters, who turn out at high rates.

questions.q: 'Policy change in Britain is best explained as punctuated equilibrium rather than incrementalism.' Discuss with reference to at least two policy areas.
markScheme: Explains incrementalism (Lindblom): bounded rationality, small changes, partisan mutual adjustment
Explains punctuated equilibrium (Baumgartner and Jones): policy monopolies, image and venue shifts, positive feedback
Hall's orders of change as a way to classify change
Case 1: macroeconomic policy (Keynesianism to monetarism, 1976–79) as a punctuation
Case 2: e.g. NHS funding or pensions as largely incremental with path dependence
Case 3: e.g. Bank of England independence (1997) or Brexit as sudden change
Considers the role of FPTP, single-party government and a centralised executive in enabling punctuations
Considers whether punctuations follow periods of gradual layering (Streeck and Thelen)
Notes the limits of both: hindsight bias, measurement of 'size' of change
Reaches a judgement: both co-exist; British institutions allow both stability and sudden change
questions.modelAnswer:
Lindblom's incrementalism holds that policy-makers with limited information and time adjust existing policy step by step. Baumgartner and Jones's punctuated equilibrium agrees that most policy is stable but argues that stability is broken by bursts of large change when new policy images and venues upset established monopolies. The question is which better fits Britain.

Macroeconomic policy shows a clear punctuation. The post-war Keynesian paradigm survived for decades through incremental adjustments to fiscal settings. Stagflation, the 1976 IMF crisis and the rise of monetarist ideas through think tanks and the press broke the monopoly of Treasury Keynesians. Thatcher's government after 1979 made what Hall (1993) calls third-order change. Bank of England operational independence in 1997, announced days after the election, was another sudden shift.

Other areas look incremental. NHS spending has risen in most years for decades, and its structure has been reorganised many times, but its founding principle of a tax-funded service, free at the point of use, has proved highly path dependent (Pierson, 2000). Pensions policy changed mostly through gradual adjustments to uprating and the state pension age, apart from the Pensions Commission's settlement in the mid-2000s.

British institutions make both patterns possible. A centralised executive with a Commons majority can impose dramatic change once the political will exists, as with the poll tax or Brexit, so punctuations may be sharper than in systems with many veto players. Yet Treasury control and departmental routines encourage incrementalism most of the time. Streeck and Thelen also warn that apparent punctuations may follow gradual 'layering' or 'drift'. Monetarism, for example, was partly prefigured by the cash limits introduced in 1976.

Punctuated equilibrium is the better overall description because it includes incrementalism as its 'equilibrium' phase while explaining the bursts of change that a majoritarian system makes possible. Even so, deciding what counts as a punctuation is largely done in hindsight.

questions.q: In 2023 the (fictional) Department for Skills launched 'SkillsFirst', a scheme to give every unemployed adult a personal training budget. Policy was designed centrally by a small team, delivered by Jobcentre staff using a new IT system, and training provided by 140 private contractors paid by course completions. Two years on, take-up is 30% of target, contractors favour short courses with high completion rates, and Jobcentre staff report they lack time to explain the scheme. Using implementation theory, explain why SkillsFirst has underperformed and recommend changes.
markScheme: Top-down analysis: unclear causal theory, insufficient resources, too many actors (Sabatier and Mazmanian; Hood's perfect administration)
Pressman and Wildavsky: multiple clearances (140 contractors, IT, Jobcentres) compound failure risk
Lipsky: street-level bureaucrats rationing time under pressure, so the scheme is deprioritised
Principal–agent problems and perverse incentives: payment by completions encourages 'creaming' and short courses (NPM gaming)
King and Crewe: design team disconnected from delivery ('cultural disconnect'), lack of piloting
Bottom-up/backward mapping (Elmore) as the remedy: design from the point of delivery
Recommendations: piloting, revised payment metrics (outcomes such as job entry, weighted for disadvantage), staff time and training, simpler IT
Overall judgement linking theory to the scenario
questions.modelAnswer:
SkillsFirst shows several classic causes of implementation failure. From a top-down view, it lacks the conditions Sabatier and Mazmanian identify: a sound causal theory, adequate resources and committed implementers. Its designers assumed that offering a budget would lead unemployed adults to train, without testing whether information, confidence or childcare were the real barriers.

Pressman and Wildavsky's arithmetic is also relevant. Success depends on a central team, an untested IT system, Jobcentre staff and 140 contractors. Even a high success rate at each link multiplies into a low chance of overall success.

The bottom-up perspective explains low take-up. Lipsky's street-level bureaucrats ration their time under pressure, so Jobcentre advisers with tight appointment schedules and benefit-compliance duties will put an optional scheme last. This policy is made at the counter, not in Whitehall.

The contracts create principal–agent problems. Paying by completions rewards contractors for 'creaming' easy learners and offering short courses, the kind of gaming Hood and others identified in New Public Management. Finally, King and Crewe's (2013) 'cultural disconnect' applies: a small central team designed the scheme without input from people who deliver or use it, and it was not piloted.

Recommendations:
- Use backward mapping (Elmore, 1979): redesign from the point of delivery with advisers and claimants.
- Pilot changes in a few areas and evaluate them before national rollout.
- Reform contractor payments to reward sustained job outcomes, with higher payments for harder-to-help groups.
- Fund dedicated adviser time or specialist coordinators and simplify the IT.

These changes match incentives to goals and accept that implementation depends as much on front-line conditions as on central design.

questions.q: 'The UK Parliament is far more powerful than the term "elective dictatorship" suggests.' Discuss.
markScheme: Explains Hailsham's elective dictatorship thesis: majority control, fusion of powers, sovereignty, weak checks
Executive dominance evidence: control of the timetable, whipping, few government defeats in normal times, secondary legislation
Russell and Cowley (2016): Parliament's influence through anticipation, behind-the-scenes pressure and amendments
Backbench rebellion and the decline of cohesion (Cowley); examples such as the 2025 welfare U-turn or Iraq 2003
Select committees after Wright (2010)
House of Lords as a revising chamber, with frequent government defeats
Hung or small-majority parliaments: the 2017–19 Parliament seized the agenda (Benn Act), defeated May's deal
Courts and constitutional limits: Miller 2017 and 2019 reinforcing Parliament
Counter-points: large majorities (1997, 2024) reduce leverage; Henry VIII powers and delegated legislation
Balanced judgement about variation by majority size and context
questions.modelAnswer:
Lord Hailsham (1976) warned that a government with a Commons majority, operating under an uncodified constitution and parliamentary sovereignty, faced few checks between elections. Formally the executive controls most Commons time, whips its MPs and rarely loses votes when it has a working majority. Much law is made through delegated legislation and Henry VIII powers, which receive little scrutiny.

Yet Russell and Cowley (2016) argue that Parliament's influence is often missed because it is exercised before votes. Ministers anticipate backbench reactions, change bills in committee and make concessions to avoid rebellions. Cowley's research shows that Labour and Conservative MPs became markedly more rebellious from the 1990s onwards. In June 2025 more than 100 Labour MPs signed a reasoned amendment against welfare cuts, and on 1 July the government dropped its planned PIP changes despite a majority of over 160. Select committees, strengthened by the Wright reforms (2010), set agendas and hold ministers to account, as in the Windrush inquiries.

The Lords also matters. Without a government majority and with many crossbenchers, it defeats governments frequently and forces amendments, although the Parliament Acts and the Salisbury convention limit it.

Parliament's power rises sharply when majorities are small. Between 2017 and 2019 the Commons rejected May's deal three times, took control of the order paper and passed the Benn Act against the government's wishes. The Supreme Court strengthened Parliament's position in Miller (2017) and Miller/Cherry (2019), insisting that the executive could not bypass it.

Still, large majorities, as in 1997 and 2024, reduce leverage, and the 2019 Johnson government passed its Withdrawal Agreement quickly. The best conclusion is that 'elective dictatorship' describes the formal potential of a majority government, but in practice Parliament constrains governments substantially through anticipation and the threat of rebellion, especially when majorities are small or the party is divided.

questions.q: In the 2026 election for the (fictional) Region of Carrick, which elects nine members to a devolved assembly using AMS (seven list seats), Party A won 7 constituencies and Party B won 2. List votes were: A 118,000; B 91,000; C 62,000; D 29,000. (a) Allocate the seven list seats using the modified D'Hondt method. (b) Compare each party's share of total seats with its share of list votes. (c) Evaluate how far AMS achieves proportionality, referring to the Scottish Parliament.
markScheme: Correctly states the divisor: list votes ÷ (constituency seats + list seats already won + 1)
Initial quotients: A 14,750; B 30,333; C 62,000; D 29,000
Allocation sequence: C, C, B, D, B, C, B
Final list seats: A 0, B 3, C 3, D 1; total seats A 7, B 5, C 3, D 1
Explains the compensatory logic: list seats correct for constituency over-representation
Limits: A remains over-represented because it won more constituencies than its proportional entitlement (no overhang correction), small regions raise the effective threshold
Scottish evidence: SNP majority in 2011 on about 44% of list votes; 'tactical' list voting and parties such as Alba trying to 'game' the system (2021)
Reaches a judgement: semi-proportional, much more than FPTP, less than pure PR
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The modified D'Hondt divisor is list votes ÷ (constituency seats + list seats already won + 1). The initial quotients are A 118,000 ÷ 8 = 14,750; B 91,000 ÷ 3 = 30,333; C 62,000 ÷ 1 = 62,000; D 29,000 ÷ 1 = 29,000. Round 1 goes to C, whose quotient becomes 31,000. Round 2 goes to C again (31,000 > 30,333), falling to 20,667. Round 3 goes to B (30,333), falling to 22,750. Round 4 goes to D (29,000), falling to 14,500. Round 5 goes to B (22,750), falling to 18,200. Round 6 goes to C (20,667), falling to 15,500. Round 7 goes to B (18,200). The list seats are A 0, B 3, C 3, D 1, and the totals are A 7, B 5, C 3, D 1.

(b) There are 300,000 list votes and 16 seats. A has 39.3% of votes against 43.8% of seats; B 30.3% against 31.2%; C 20.7% against 18.8%; D 9.7% against 6.2%.

(c) The list tier sharply reduces disproportionality. Under FPTP alone, A would hold 7 of 9 seats (78%) with under 40% of the vote. A remains over-represented because its constituency haul exceeds its proportional entitlement and AMS here has no overhang compensation. With only seven list seats per region, a small party needs roughly 5–6% of the regional vote to win a seat, which is a high effective threshold.

The Scottish Parliament shows these limits. In 2011 the SNP won an outright majority (69 of 129) on about 44% of the list vote, despite AMS being designed to make majorities unlikely. In 2021 Alba tried to exploit the list tier by asking SNP voters to switch their list vote, though it won no seats. AMS is therefore semi-proportional: far fairer than FPTP but short of full PR.

questions.q: 'Class has been replaced by age and education as the basis of British electoral politics.' Critically evaluate.
markScheme: Sets out the class-alignment era: Pulzer (1967); Butler and Stokes (1969); Alford index
Dealignment evidence: Särlvik and Crewe; decline in absolute class voting
Heath, Jowell and Curtice: relative class voting declined less; the debate over measurement
Age divide: 2017 and 2019 age as the strongest predictor (e.g. a crossover age around the late 30s or 40s in 2019)
Education divide: graduates v non-graduates, linked to values (Sobolewska and Ford 2020; Surridge)
Brexit as accelerator: Leave/Remain identities (Hobolt, Leeper and Tilley 2021)
Realignment, not just dealignment: working-class voters shifting to the Conservatives and Reform; Labour's middle-class base
Class persists in different forms: economic left-right attitudes, the 2024 Reform vote, income and housing tenure
Considers whether age partly reflects housing and assets, so material interests remain
2024 complicates: fragmentation, Labour's vote fell among young voters to Greens and independents, Reform's older non-graduate base
Considers political supply: parties choose which divides to mobilise (Evans and Tilley 2017)
Reaches a nuanced judgement
questions.modelAnswer:
In 1967 Pulzer wrote that class was the basis of British party politics, and Butler and Stokes (1969) showed that class shaped inherited party identification. From the 1970s, Särlvik and Crewe (1983) documented class dealignment as the share of manual workers voting Labour fell. Heath, Jowell and Curtice (1985) argued that relative class voting, measured by odds ratios, fell less than absolute measures implied, since much of the change reflected a shrinking manual working class.

By 2017 and 2019, age and education had become the strongest predictors. In 2019 younger voters favoured Labour heavily while those over 65 voted Conservative by large margins, and class predicted vote choice only weakly. Graduates leaned towards Labour and the Liberal Democrats, and non-graduates towards the Conservatives. Sobolewska and Ford (2020) link this to an identity conflict between graduate 'identity liberals' and older non-graduate 'identity conservatives' over immigration, diversity and national identity. Brexit accelerated the change: Hobolt, Leeper and Tilley (2021) show that Leave and Remain became identities, and the 2019 'red wall' gains reflected working-class Leavers moving to the Conservatives.

That suggests realignment rather than the end of class. Evans and Tilley (2017) argue that class voting declined largely because Labour moved to the centre and stopped offering working-class voters a distinct choice. Economic left–right attitudes still predict vote choice, and the class divide has reversed direction on the cultural dimension rather than disappearing. Age is also partly material: housing tenure and wealth separate older owners from younger renters, so generational voting reflects economic interest as well as values.

The 2024 election complicates the picture. Labour won with a fragmented coalition, losing young voters to the Greens and independents. Reform UK's 14% drew heavily on older, non-graduate, working-class voters, so the radical right now competes for a class constituency.

Overall, the statement captures a real shift in the best predictors of vote choice, but 'replaced' overstates it. Class has been reshaped by education, age and assets, and party strategy determines which divides are mobilised.

questions.q: 'The Conservative and Labour parties are now electoral coalitions under threat rather than ideological movements.' Discuss with reference to developments since 2015.
markScheme: Defines the concepts: catch-all (Kirchheimer) and electoral-professional parties v ideological mass parties
Conservatives: Thatcherite economics, one-nation tradition, national populism after Brexit; 2019 coalition of affluent and 'red wall' voters
Conservatives' collapse in 2024 to 121 seats and loss of votes to Reform UK; leadership instability (four PMs 2016–22)
Labour: Corbyn's (2015–20) ideological revival and mass membership surge
Starmer's repositioning: 'changed Labour', fiscal rules, removal of Corbyn; 2024 victory on 33.7%
Labour's coalition fragility: Greens, Gaza-related independents, Reform in working-class seats
Membership-driven leadership contests pull towards ideology (Truss 2022)
Fragmentation and the effective number of parties
FPTP preserving the two-party structure in seats
Reasoned judgement: both are factional coalitions with real ideological traditions, and both are vulnerable
questions.modelAnswer:
Kirchheimer's catch-all thesis predicted that mass parties would weaken their ideological identities to compete for broad electorates. Events since 2015 show both main British parties combining ideological revival with fragile electoral coalitions.

Labour's recent history shows ideology. Under Corbyn (2015–20), membership surged past half a million and the party moved sharply left, promising to nationalise utilities and raise taxes on the wealthy. The 2019 defeat, Labour's worst since 1935, prompted Starmer to reposition it as 'changed Labour', with tight fiscal rules and a focus on security. The 2024 landslide rested on just 33.7% of the vote and an efficient spread across seats rather than wide enthusiasm. Labour has since lost ground to the Greens, pro-Gaza independents and Reform UK in post-industrial seats, which shows a fragile coalition.

The Conservatives have moved from coalition-building to crisis. Johnson's 2019 victory joined affluent southern voters with working-class Leavers in the 'red wall' around 'Get Brexit Done'. That coalition broke apart under three prime ministers (Johnson, Truss and Sunak) in under five years. Truss's 2022 mini-budget, chosen by a membership more ideological than voters (Bale, Webb and Poletti, 2020), damaged the party's reputation for economic competence. In 2024 the Conservatives fell to 121 seats, losing Leave voters to Reform and liberal voters to the Liberal Democrats.

The statement therefore captures something real. Both parties' vote shares are historically low, the effective number of electoral parties has risen, and Reform's poll leads in 2025 threatened both. But both parties remain ideological in their factions and members: Thatcherite, one-nation and national-populist strands among Conservatives, and the socialist left and Labour right. FPTP still protects their combined dominance in seats.

The best conclusion is that the two main parties are now fragile coalitions in which ideological factions compete. The threat comes less from a loss of ideology than from a changing electorate that FPTP increasingly struggles to channel.

questions.q: 'Devolution has strengthened rather than weakened the Union.' Discuss.
markScheme: Sets out the 1990s argument that devolution would kill nationalism 'stone dead' (George Robertson) v Tam Dalyell's West Lothian warnings
Evidence for strengthening: support for the institutions; 2014 No vote (55.3%); Northern Ireland peace and power-sharing
Evidence for weakening: SNP dominance since 2007, independence support around half, the 2014 referendum itself
Constitutional friction: Sewel convention breached over Brexit (EU Withdrawal Act 2018 without consent); Internal Market Act 2020; section 35 order 2023
2022 Supreme Court reference preventing a unilateral referendum: Union upheld by law, not consent
Northern Ireland: repeated collapses; Protocol and Windsor Framework strains; demographic and electoral change (Sinn Féin largest party)
Wales: growing support for devolution; independence remains a minority position
England: the English question; asymmetric arrangements
Theory: union state (Rokkan and Urwin), quasi-federalism, Bogdanor
Reasoned judgement distinguishing institutional stability from constitutional legitimacy
questions.modelAnswer:
Labour's George Robertson predicted that devolution would kill nationalism 'stone dead', while sceptics such as Tam Dalyell warned it would be a slippery slope. A quarter of a century later, the evidence is mixed.

The case for strengthening is substantial. Devolved institutions have become very popular, and almost no one in Scotland or Wales wants them abolished. By giving different nations real self-government within the UK, devolution fits the 'union state' tradition of Rokkan and Urwin, in which nations keep distinct institutions. Scotland voted No to independence in 2014 by 55.3%, which suggests that devolution offered an acceptable middle path. In Northern Ireland, power-sharing under the Good Friday Agreement has replaced violence with institutional politics, despite repeated suspensions.

The case for weakening is also strong. Devolution gave the SNP a platform: it has governed since 2007 and won a majority in 2011 that led to the 2014 referendum. Support for independence has hovered around half in many polls since. Brexit intensified tensions. Scotland and Northern Ireland voted Remain, the EU (Withdrawal) Act 2018 passed without Holyrood's consent despite Sewel, and the Internal Market Act 2020 limited devolved policy choices. In 2023 the first section 35 order blocked a Holyrood bill. The 2022 Supreme Court ruling that Holyrood cannot legislate for a referendum upholds the Union in law, but it also shows that the Union depends partly on legal limits rather than consent. In Northern Ireland, the institutions collapsed in 2017–20 and 2022–24, and Sinn Féin is now the largest party at Stormont, local and Westminster levels.

The English question remains unresolved, since England lacks a voice of its own and the arrangements are asymmetric.

On balance, devolution has given the UK durable institutions and probably prevented an earlier break-up. However, it has made the Union depend on continuing consent in each nation, so its strength now depends on how the centre manages relations with the devolved governments.

questions.q: 'Brexit was the product of long-term structural change rather than a short-term campaign.' Critically evaluate this explanation of the 2016 referendum result.
markScheme: Structural 'left behind' thesis: Ford and Goodwin (2014); Goodwin and Heath (2016)
Values and education divide: Sobolewska and Ford (2020); Hobolt (2016)
Long-run Euroscepticism: the press, the Conservative party's internal divide since Maastricht, UKIP's rise
Immigration after 2004 EU enlargement as a salient long-term grievance
Austerity: Fetzer (2019) linked welfare cuts to UKIP and Leave support
Short-term factors: Vote Leave's 'take back control' and £350m message; the leaders effect (Johnson, Gove)
Clarke, Goodwin and Whiteley (2017): cost–benefit and risk calculations, emotions and leaders
Remain campaign weaknesses: 'Project Fear' and Corbyn's lukewarm involvement
Cameron's decision to hold the referendum: an elite choice, not a structural inevitability
Counterfactual reasoning: a narrow margin means small factors could have swung it
Reaches a judgement integrating structure, agency and contingency
questions.modelAnswer:
The structural account is powerful. Ford and Goodwin (2014) traced UKIP's rise to 'left behind' voters: older, white, non-graduate and living in declining post-industrial towns. Goodwin and Heath (2016) found these groups voted Leave in large numbers. Hobolt (2016) and Sobolewska and Ford (2020) stress values more than income: education, authoritarian attitudes, English identity and hostility to immigration predicted Leave best. These divides had grown for decades through educational expansion, deindustrialisation and the large rise in EU migration after the 2004 enlargement. Fetzer (2019) argues that austerity after 2010 increased support for UKIP and Leave in the areas hit hardest. Euroscepticism had divided the Conservative party since Maastricht and was nurtured by much of the press.

Structure alone cannot explain the result. A 51.9% to 48.1% margin means that a shift of fewer than two percentage points would have reversed it. The referendum itself was a choice: Cameron promised it in 2013 to manage his party and UKIP, not because structural forces required it. Clarke, Goodwin and Whiteley (2017) show that campaign-period judgements of risk, benefit and leaders affected individual votes. Vote Leave's 'take back control' message turned diverse grievances into one appeal about sovereignty and immigration, and Johnson's involvement gave it a popular face. Remain's economic warnings were dismissed as 'Project Fear', and Labour's half-hearted campaign under Corbyn failed to mobilise its supporters.

The best explanation combines both. Long-term changes created a large constituency ready to vote Leave, which shows why the result was possible and why it split Britain along education and age lines. Elite choices and the campaign explain why the referendum happened and why Leave narrowly won. The statement sets up a false choice: structure created the conditions, while agency and contingency settled the outcome.

questions.q: 'The British welfare state has been transformed since 1979.' Assess this claim using Pierson's theory of retrenchment.
markScheme: Explains Pierson (1994): new politics of welfare; retrenchment is harder than expansion; blame avoidance
Thatcher: limited success cutting core programmes; council house sales (Right to Buy 1980); price uprating of pensions from 1980
Systemic or hidden retrenchment: weakening future support through indexation and institutional change
New Labour: tax credits, minimum wage, welfare-to-work (New Deal); social investment
Coalition and Conservative austerity: benefit freeze, benefit cap, Universal Credit, two-child limit; working-age cuts
Protection of pensioners: triple lock (2011) showing Pierson's electoral constraint
NHS remains universal and tax-funded, a sign of path dependence
Conditionality and sanctions as a qualitative transformation
Considers alternative accounts: Hall's paradigm shift; Taylor-Gooby's new social risks
Reaches a judgement: incremental cuts and recalibration, not wholesale transformation
questions.modelAnswer:
Pierson (1994) argued that cutting welfare follows different politics from building it. Programmes create concentrated constituencies, voters punish visible losses more than they reward savings, and governments therefore use blame-avoidance strategies: hidden cuts, delayed effects and reductions targeted at weak groups. His study of Thatcher and Reagan found that core programmes largely survived.

The British evidence partly supports him. Despite her ideology, Thatcher did not dismantle the NHS or the state pension, and social spending as a share of GDP was not substantially lower when she left office. Her most significant changes were less visible or 'systemic': linking pensions to prices rather than earnings from 1980 reduced their relative value over time, and the Right to Buy shrank social housing. These are exactly the hidden techniques Pierson described.

Later governments made more change than Pierson's account implies. New Labour added tax credits, a minimum wage and the New Deal, shifting towards 'activating' social investment. After 2010 austerity brought real cuts to working-age support: a benefit freeze, the benefit cap, the two-child limit and Universal Credit with stricter conditionality and sanctions. These changes altered the welfare state for people of working age. The 2025 retreat on disability cuts and the decision to lift the two-child limit show how hard further cuts remain politically.

Pensioners were protected throughout. The triple lock since 2011 has raised the state pension's relative value, supporting Pierson's argument about electoral constraint, since older voters turn out heavily. The NHS remains universal and tax-funded.

The welfare state has therefore been recalibrated rather than transformed. Working-age support has become more targeted, conditional and less generous, while pensions and healthcare have been protected. Pierson underestimated how far determined governments can cut support for groups with low electoral power, but he was right that wholesale dismantling of popular programmes has not happened.

questions.q: In 2025 the (fictional) Ministry of Social Security proposes to cut the Universal Credit taper rate from 55% to 45%. Molly works 20 hours a week, earning £1,000 a month (below the income tax and NI thresholds, so her gross and net pay are the same), and her work allowance is £400. Her maximum UC award is £900. (a) Calculate her UC payment under each taper. (b) Evaluate the policy's likely effects on work incentives and fiscal cost.
markScheme: States Molly gains £60 a month; total monthly income of £1,570 v £1,630
Explains the marginal effective tax rate: she keeps 55p per extra £1 rather than 45p; notes that the taper applies to net pay, so once tax and NI are paid the combined rate is higher
Work incentive argument: stronger incentive to increase hours; reduces the poverty trap
Costs: higher spending; extends UC entitlement further up the income scale
Evaluation: evidence on behavioural responses is mixed; incentives also depend on childcare, health and available hours
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) At a 55% taper, earnings above the work allowance are £1,000 − £400 = £600, so UC is reduced by 0.55 × £600 = £330. Molly receives £900 − £330 = £570, giving monthly income of £1,570 (she pays no income tax or NI at this level). At 45% the reduction is 0.45 × £600 = £270, so UC is £630 and income is £1,630, a gain of £60 a month.

(b) The taper is part of the marginal effective tax rate. At 55%, Molly keeps 45p of each extra pound earned above the allowance while she is below the tax and NI thresholds. Because the taper is applied to net pay, a basic-rate taxpayer paying 20% tax and 8% NI keeps only 45% of the remaining 72p, about 32p, a marginal effective tax rate of about 68%. Cutting the taper to 45% lets her keep 55p (about 40p once she pays tax and NI), strengthening the incentive to work more hours and easing the poverty trap that Universal Credit was meant to reduce.

The policy has costs. Every working claimant above the allowance gains, and entitlement extends to people on higher earnings, so the cost is significant. The 2021 cut from 63% to 55%, together with higher work allowances, was costed at roughly £2 billion a year. Its effect on work incentives may also be modest. Many claimants face constraints such as caring responsibilities, ill health, childcare costs and employers' limits on hours, so they cannot respond to better incentives. Some benefits go to people who would have worked more anyway. Supporters counter that the change rewards work and helps low-paid families with the cost of living. Overall, a lower taper would raise incomes for working claimants and improve incentives at the margin, but its value for money depends on how many people actually increase their hours.

questions.q: The (fictional) Prime Minister Helen Ashworth leads a government with a Commons majority of 12. Her Planning Reform Bill would remove local authorities' power to block housing developments of more than 500 homes. Forty of her own MPs, mostly from rural seats, have signed a letter opposing it; the Lords has a large non-government majority; and the relevant select committee has published a critical report. Analyse the constraints Ashworth faces in passing the bill and the strategies available to her.
markScheme: Arithmetic: a majority of 12 means about 7 rebels voting with the opposition can defeat the bill
Party management: whips, patronage, the threat of the whip's removal, constituency pressures on rural MPs
Anticipated reactions and concessions before votes (Russell and Cowley)
Lords constraints: amendments, ping-pong, delay; the Parliament Acts as a last resort; the Salisbury convention if it was a manifesto commitment
Select committee: no veto but agenda and legitimacy effects; the government must respond
Strategies: amendments (thresholds, local consultation), framing as a manifesto pledge or confidence matter, cross-party support
Context: PM's authority depends on electoral standing and party confidence (Heffernan)
Reasoned conclusion on likely outcome and best strategy
questions.modelAnswer:
With a majority of 12, Ashworth can be defeated if just seven of her MPs vote with a united opposition, or slightly more if some abstain. Forty potential rebels therefore pose a real threat. Rural MPs face constituency pressure on housing, so the usual tools of party management, such as whipping, promises of promotion and the threat of removing the whip, may not be enough. Removing the whip would in any case further reduce her majority.

Russell and Cowley (2016) show that parliamentary influence usually works through anticipated reactions. The likeliest result is concessions before the vote: raising the 500-home threshold, adding a statutory consultation duty or protecting green-belt land.

The Lords is a second constraint. With a large non-government majority, it can amend the bill and send it back repeatedly in 'ping-pong'. If the reform was in the manifesto, the Salisbury convention means peers should not block it at second reading, but they can still revise it. The Parliament Acts allow the Commons to override the Lords only after about a year's delay, which is costly in time.

The select committee's critical report has no veto but gives rebels authoritative arguments and media coverage, and the government must formally respond. Heffernan's view of prime ministerial power as contingent matters too: if Ashworth is polling well, rebels are less willing to defy her.

Her best strategy combines negotiation and framing. She should offer targeted amendments to split the rebels, present the bill as essential to a manifesto housing pledge and possibly seek opposition support if Labour-style parties favour housebuilding. Making it a confidence matter would be high risk with such a small majority. The likely outcome is a diluted but passed bill.

questions.q: 'Brexit exposed the tension between popular sovereignty and parliamentary sovereignty in the UK constitution.' Discuss.
markScheme: Defines parliamentary sovereignty (Dicey) and popular sovereignty (referendums as expressions of the people's will)
The 2016 referendum was legally advisory (the 2015 Act set no legal consequence) but politically binding
Miller (2017): Parliament, not the executive, had to authorise Article 50, reaffirming parliamentary sovereignty
2017–19 Parliament: MPs, mostly Remain supporters, asked to deliver Leave; defeats of May's deal; indicative votes
Benn Act and Parliament taking control of the order paper; accusations of 'Parliament v the people'
Miller/Cherry (2019): prorogation unlawful; courts protecting Parliament
The 2019 election resolved the deadlock through electoral rather than constitutional means
Wider significance: referendums becoming constitutional conventions on key questions; implications for devolution (Scotland)
Reasoned judgement
questions.modelAnswer:
Dicey's doctrine of parliamentary sovereignty holds that Parliament can make or unmake any law and that no other body can override it. Referendums introduce a rival principle, popular sovereignty, in which the people decide directly. Brexit brought these principles into conflict.

The European Union Referendum Act 2015 set no legal consequence for the result, so the vote was advisory in law. Politically, however, Cameron's government promised to implement it, and both main parties pledged in 2017 to respect it. In Miller (2017) the Supreme Court held that triggering Article 50 required an Act of Parliament because withdrawal would change domestic law. Ministers could not use the prerogative to implement the people's vote without Parliament.

The conflict was sharpest in the 2017–19 Parliament. Most MPs had backed Remain but were asked to deliver Leave. They rejected May's deal three times, took control of the order paper for indicative votes and passed the Benn Act to prevent a no-deal exit. Supporters saw this as Parliament doing its job. Critics, including Johnson's government, framed it as 'Parliament versus the people'. Johnson's attempt to prorogue Parliament for five weeks was ruled unlawful in Miller/Cherry (2019). The courts upheld parliamentary sovereignty and parliamentary accountability against the executive.

In the end the tension was resolved politically. The December 2019 election gave Johnson an 80-seat majority, and Parliament quickly passed his Withdrawal Agreement. An election reconciled the people's mandate with Parliament's.

Brexit suggests that referendums on major constitutional questions have created a political convention that their results must be implemented, even though Parliament remains legally sovereign. The same tension appears in debates over Scottish independence. The constitution coped, but only by showing that legal and political sovereignty can diverge.
